📖 Chapter Notes, Concepts, Tips & Tricks (Class 10 Light) ▼
💡 1. Nature of Light ⭐ Core
Light travels in straight lines (rectilinear propagation) — proven by sharp shadows.
When light falls on an object, it is reflected; this reflected light entering our eyes makes objects visible.
Diffraction: When light passes a very small opaque obstacle, it bends slightly around it.
Modern quantum theory: light is neither purely wave nor purely particle — it has dual nature.
Speed of light in vacuum: c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s (fastest possible speed).
🪞 2. Laws of Reflection ⭐ Must Learn
Law 1: Angle of incidence (i) = Angle of reflection (r).
Law 2: Incident ray, normal at the point of incidence, and reflected ray — all lie in the same plane.
These laws apply to all reflecting surfaces — plane, spherical (concave/convex), and any other shape.
∠i = ∠r
✅ Plane mirror image properties: virtual, erect, same size as object, laterally inverted, image distance = object distance.
⚪ 3. Spherical Mirrors ⭐ Core
Concave mirror: Reflecting surface curved inwards (towards centre). Converging mirror. Used in torches, headlights, shaving, dentist.
Convex mirror: Reflecting surface curved outwards. Diverging mirror. Used as rear-view mirror.
Pole (P): Centre of reflecting surface.
Centre of Curvature (C): Centre of the sphere of which mirror is a part. Outside the mirror.
Radius of Curvature (R): Distance PC = R.
Principal Axis: Line through P and C, normal to mirror at P.
Principal Focus (F): Point where parallel rays converge (concave) or appear to diverge from (convex).
Focal Length (f): Distance PF.
R = 2f   ⇒   f = R / 2
⚠️ Concave mirror: F in front of mirror. Convex mirror: F behind mirror.

📏 5. Ray Rules & Sign Convention (Mirrors) ⭐ Critical
Rule 1: Parallel to principal axis → passes through F (concave) / appears to come from F (convex).
Rule 2: Through F (concave) / directed towards F (convex) → emerges parallel to principal axis.
Rule 3: Through C (concave) / directed towards C (convex) → reflects back along same path.
Rule 4: Incident at pole P obliquely → reflects with ∠i = ∠r.
New Cartesian Sign Convention:
Pole (P) = origin. Principal axis = x-axis.
Object always on left of mirror.
Distances to right of P = +ve. To left = −ve.
Heights above axis = +ve. Below = −ve.
fconcave = −ve   |   fconvex = +ve
🧮 6. Mirror Formula & Magnification ⭐ Formula
1/v + 1/u = 1/f
Valid for ALL spherical mirrors, ALL object positions (with proper sign convention).
m = h′/h = −v/u
m negative (m < 0): real, inverted image.
m positive (m > 0): virtual, erect image.
|m| > 1: enlarged  |  |m| < 1: diminished  |  |m| = 1: same size.
🌊 7. Refraction & Refractive Index ⭐ Core
Refraction: Bending of light when it travels obliquely from one transparent medium to another — due to change in speed.
Laws of Refraction:
Law 1: Incident ray, refracted ray, and normal at point of incidence — all in same plane.
Law 2 (Snell's Law): sin i / sin r = constant = n₂₁ (for given colour and pair of media).
sin i / sin r = n₂₁ = v₁ / v₂
Rarer → Denser: bends towards normal, speed decreases.
Denser → Rarer: bends away from normal, speed increases.
n = c / v = (speed in vacuum) / (speed in medium)
Absolute refractive index (n): n ≥ 1 always (n_air ≈ 1.0003, n_water = 1.33, n_glass = 1.50, n_diamond = 2.42).
Optical density ≠ mass density. Higher refractive index = optically denser. E.g., kerosene (n=1.44) is optically denser than water (n=1.33) though its mass density is less.
🔍 8. Spherical Lenses ⭐ Core
Convex (converging) lens: thicker at middle. Converges parallel rays to a point.
Concave (diverging) lens: thicker at edges. Diverges parallel rays.
Optical centre (O): Central point; ray through O passes undeviated.
Principal foci F₁, F₂ on either side of lens. Focal length f = OF.
Ray Rules:
1. Parallel ray → through F on other side (convex) / appears from F (concave).
2. Through F → emerges parallel to principal axis.
3. Through optical centre O → no deviation.
Image Table – Convex Lens (Table 9.4):
ObjectImageSizeNature
At ∞At F₂PointReal, inverted
Beyond 2F₁F₂ to 2F₂DiminishedReal, inverted

F₁ to 2F₁Beyond 2F₂EnlargedReal, inverted

Concave Lens (Table 9.5): ALWAYS virtual, erect, diminished — irrespective of object position.
⚡ 9. Lens Formula, Magnification & Power ⭐ Formula
1/v − 1/u = 1/f
Valid for ALL spherical lenses (sign convention from optical centre).
m = h′/h = v/u
m < 0: real, inverted.    m > 0: virtual, erect.
⚠️ Lens magnification = v/u (NO minus sign). Mirror magnification = −v/u (with minus sign). Very common confusion!
Power of a Lens:
P = 1 / f (f in metres)
SI unit: dioptre (D). 1 D = 1 m⁻¹.
1 dioptre = power of a lens whose focal length is 1 metre.
Convex lens: P > 0 (f +ve). Concave lens: P < 0 (f −ve).
Combination of Lenses in Contact:
P = P₁ + P₂ + …   ⇒   1/f = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂ + …
🔭 10. Applications – Eye, Prism, Telescope ⭐ 2026 Focus
Hypermetropia (far-sightedness): image of nearby object forms behind retina. Causes: eyeball too short, focal length of eye lens too long. Corrected by convex lens.
Myopia (near-sightedness): image of distant object forms in front of retina. Corrected by concave lens.
Prism refraction: ray bends twice — at entry and exit. Angle of deviation (D) is angle between incident and emergent ray. Reversing path → same deviation.
Reflecting Telescope: Uses large concave mirror as objective + plane mirror to redirect + convex lens as eyepiece. Observer sees virtual, magnified, inverted image. Mirrors avoid chromatic aberration of lenses.
✅ Advantage of convex mirror as rear-view: wider field of view + always erect, diminished image.

💡 Highest optical density: Diamond (2.42). Lowest (from table): Air (1.0003) / Ice (1.31).
Light travels fastest in rarer medium (lowest n) and slowest in denser medium (highest n).
🎯 12. Exam Tips, Tricks & Common Mistakes ⚠️ Must Read
🔑 Sign Convention Cheat-Sheet: Always start u with −ve (object on left). Mirror: f negative for concave, positive for convex. Lens: f negative for concave, positive for convex.
🔑 Mirror vs Lens m: Mirror m = −v/u (with minus). Lens m = v/u (no minus). Don't mix these!
🔑 R = 2f always. If R given, halve it to get f, then use formula.
❌ Mistake 1: Saying convex mirror forms real image. It NEVER does — always virtual, erect, diminished.
❌ Mistake 2: Using m = v/u for mirrors. Must be −v/u.
❌ Mistake 3: Forgetting to convert cm → m before computing Power (P = 1/f with f in metres).
❌ Mistake 4: Confusing "optically denser" with "mass denser". Use refractive index comparison.
❌ Mistake 5: In prism, measuring angle with surface instead of normal — always use normal.
✅ Speed Trick 1: If |m| = 1 for real image, object at 2F (both mirror & lens).
✅ Speed Trick 2: For convex mirror, image is ALWAYS between P and F, virtual, diminished — no calculation needed.
✅ Speed Trick 3: For concave mirror, virtual erect enlarged image ⇔ object between P and F.
✅ Speed Trick 4: Lens combination P = P₁ + P₂. The sign of net P tells you converging (+) or diverging (−).
📝 Ray diagram scoring: Always label P, F, C (or 2F), arrows on rays, and mark object and image heights.
📝 Numerical scoring: Write Given, Formula, Substitution, Answer with unit — even if answer is wrong, steps get marks.

Weightage: 35.0%34 Questions (70 Marks)

🥉 Priority 3: Refraction & Refractive Index
Weightage: 19.5%17 Questions (39 Marks)

Master Snell's law $\sin i / \sin r = n_{21}$, optical density vs mass density, and glass slab lateral displacement.

🎯 Exam Tips & Observations
  • Ray Arrows: Always draw arrows on incident and reflected/refracted rays.
  • Sign Traps: $u$ is ALWAYS negative; $f$ is negative for concave and positive for convex.
  • Power Conversion: Convert focal length from cm to meters before calculating $P = 1/f$.
  • 2F Repetition: Convex lens image at $2F$ has recurred across 2026, 2024, 2022, 2020.
